title: Introduction to MLOps
summary: MLOps applies DevOps principles to machine learning, addressing the unique challenges of data and models that change over time. It covers versioning data and models, building reproducible pipelines, automating training and deployment, and monitoring
content:
# Introduction to MLOps ##### The model that was 94% accurate eleven months ago A retailer deployed a demand forecasting model with 94% accuracy on its test set. It went live in March and nobody touched it again. By February the following year, buyers had stopped trusting it. Investigation showed accuracy had fallen to 71% — not suddenly, but gradually, month by month. Two new product categories had launched that the model had never seen. Post-pandemic buying patterns had shifted. A supplier change had altered lead times, which fed one of the input features. Nobody noticed because nobody was measuring. There was no monitoring, no scheduled retraining, and — critically — **no way to retrain**. The engineer who built it had left, the training data had been assembled by hand in a notebook, and the exact preprocessing steps existed only in that notebook's execution order, which no longer ran. The model was not the failure. The **absence of a lifecycle around it** was. Sculley et al. (2015) called this hidden technical debt: ML code is a small box in a much larger system of data collection, verification, serving infrastructure and monitoring, and teams routinely build the box while neglecting everything around it. ##### What MLOps is **MLOps** is the practice of reliably building, deploying and maintaining machine learning systems in production. It borrows from DevOps and adds what DevOps does not address: **data and models as first-class versioned artifacts**. Kreuzberger et al. (2022) define it through four principles worth holding onto: **Reproducibility** — any past result can be recreated exactly. **Automation** — the path from data to deployed model runs without manual steps. **Continuous monitoring** — performance is observed in production, not assumed. **Collaboration** — data scientists, engineers and operations work in one system. ##### How MLOps differs from DevOps This is today's assignment, and the distinction is substantive rather than terminological. | | DevOps | MLOps | |---|---|---| | Versioned artifacts | Code | **Code + data + model + config** | | Testing | Deterministic — passes or fails | **Statistical** — accuracy thresholds | | "Correct" behaviour | Specified in advance | **Learned from data, discovered empirically** | | Degradation over time | Code does not decay | **Models decay as the world changes** | | Deployment artifact | Binary or container | Container **plus model weights plus data lineage** | | Rollback | Revert the commit | Revert code **and** model **and** possibly data | | Team | Developers, ops | Data scientists, ML engineers, ops, domain experts | Three differences carry most of the weight. **Data is a dependency.** Traditional software depends on code and libraries; ML depends additionally on training data. Change the data and the behaviour changes, even with identical code. So data must be versioned exactly as code is — which is what DVC provides. **Testing is statistical.** A unit test asserts `add(2, 2) == 4`. An ML test asserts `accuracy > 0.85 on the holdout set` — a threshold, on a distribution, that can pass today and fail tomorrow with the same code. **Models degrade without being touched.** This is the property with no software analogue. A correctly functioning web service behaves the same in year two as in year one. A correctly functioning model gets worse, because the world it was trained on moves away from it. That last point has two named forms, developed properly on monitoring day but worth defining here: **Data drift** — the input distribution changes. Customers get younger; a new product category appears; a sensor is recalibrated. The relationship between features and target is intact, but the model now sees inputs unlike its training data. **Concept drift** — the relationship itself changes. What predicted fraud in 2024 does not predict fraud in 2026, because fraudsters adapted. Even with identical inputs, the correct output has changed. The retailer suffered both simultaneously, which is typical. ##### The production ML lifecycle ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Data sources] --> B[Ingestion
+ validation] B --> C[Feature engineering] C --> D[Training] D --> E[Evaluation
against thresholds] E -->|fails| C E -->|passes| F[Model registry
staging] F --> G[Deploy: shadow →
canary → full] G --> H[Serving] H --> I[Monitoring:
drift + performance] I -->|drift detected| J[Retraining trigger] J --> C I -->|degradation| K[Rollback to
previous version] K --> H ``` The loops distinguish this from a linear project. **Every arrow that goes backwards is something that must be automated**, or it will not happen — as the retailer discovered. ##### Data and model versioning with DVC Git handles code well and binary files badly. A 2 GB dataset committed to Git makes every clone 2 GB and every change stores another full copy. **DVC (Data Version Control)** solves this by storing a small **pointer file** in Git and the actual data in external storage — S3, GCS, or a network drive. You get `git checkout` semantics for datasets. ```bash pip install "dvc[s3]" dvc init dvc remote add -d storage s3://my-bucket/dvc-store # Track a dataset — DVC moves it to cache and creates data/raw.csv.dvc dvc add data/raw/transactions.csv git add data/raw/transactions.csv.dvc data/raw/.gitignore git commit -m "data: add transaction dataset v1 (84k rows)" dvc push # upload to remote storage # On another machine, or after checking out an old commit git checkout v1.0 dvc pull # fetches the EXACT data for that commit ``` The pointer file is tiny and human-readable: ```yaml # data/raw/transactions.csv.dvc outs: - md5: a7f3c2e891b4d5f6a2c8e1b9d4f7a3c2 size: 2147483648 path: transactions.csv ``` That MD5 hash is the mechanism. Git stores the hash; DVC resolves it to the actual bytes. Checking out a commit from six months ago and running `dvc pull` gives you **exactly the data that produced that result** — which is precisely what the retailer could not do. ##### Reproducible pipelines DVC also defines pipelines as a dependency graph. Each stage declares its inputs and outputs, and DVC re-runs only what changed. ```yaml # dvc.yaml stages: prepare: cmd: python src/prepare.py deps: - src/prepare.py - data/raw/transactions.csv outs: - data/processed/clean.parquet features: cmd: python src/features.py deps: - src/features.py - data/processed/clean.parquet params: - features.window_days - features.min_transactions outs: - data/features/train.parquet - data/features/test.parquet train: cmd: python src/train.py deps: - src/train.py - data/features/train.parquet params: - train.n_estimators - train.max_depth - train.learning_rate outs: - models/model.joblib metrics: - metrics/train.json: cache: false evaluate: cmd: python src/evaluate.py deps: - src/evaluate.py - models/model.joblib - data/features/test.parquet metrics: - metrics/eval.json: cache: false plots: - plots/confusion_matrix.json ``` ```yaml # params.yaml — hyperparameters, versioned in Git features: window_days: 90 min_transactions: 3 train: n_estimators: 300 max_depth: 12 learning_rate: 0.05 ``` ```bash dvc repro # runs only stages whose deps changed dvc metrics show # current metrics dvc metrics diff main # compare against another branch dvc params diff # what parameters changed dvc dag # visualize the pipeline ``` The **caching** behaviour is the practical benefit. Change `train.max_depth` and `dvc repro` skips `prepare` and `features` entirely, running only `train` and `evaluate`. On a pipeline where feature engineering takes twenty minutes, that turns an experiment cycle from half an hour into two minutes. The **reproducibility** benefit is stronger still. `git checkout && dvc pull && dvc repro` recreates any historical result — same data, same parameters, same code, same output. ##### Model registry and staging The registry manages which model is production, separately from experiments. ```python import mlflow client = mlflow.MlflowClient() version = mlflow.register_model(f"runs:/{run_id}/model", "fraud-detector") # Aliases rather than hard-coded version numbers client.set_registered_model_alias("fraud-detector", "staging", version.version) client.set_model_version_tag("fraud-detector", version.version, "data_version", data_hash) client.set_model_version_tag("fraud-detector", version.version, "git_commit", git_sha) # After validation passes, promote client.set_registered_model_alias("fraud-detector", "champion", version.version) # Production loads by alias model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/fraud-detector@champion") ``` Using an **alias** rather than a version number means promotion and rollback are registry operations, not code deployments. Reverting a bad model becomes one command that takes effect immediately. The staged rollout that follows is worth naming: **Shadow** — the new model runs alongside the current one, receiving real traffic, but its predictions are logged rather than used. You compare against the incumbent on live data with zero risk. **Canary** — 5% of traffic goes to the new model. Watch the metrics. **Full** — promote to 100%, keeping the previous version available for instant rollback. ##### MLOps maturity levels Google's widely-cited framing, with a fourth level worth adding: **Level 0 — manual.** Notebooks, manual training, manual deployment, no monitoring. The model is a one-off artifact. This is where the retailer was. **Level 1 — ML pipeline automation.** Training is a reproducible pipeline (DVC or similar), experiments are tracked, models are registered, and retraining can be triggered. Deployment is still manual. **Level 2 — CI/CD automation.** Code commits trigger automated testing, training, validation and deployment. Retraining is triggered by drift detection or schedule, with automated rollback. **Level 3 — full automation.** Continuous training, automated feature stores, automated drift response, self-healing. The realistic advice: **most teams should target level 1 and stop.** It captures the majority of the value — reproducibility and traceability — for a fraction of the effort. Level 2 becomes worthwhile when you have several models in production or retrain frequently. Level 3 is for organizations running ML at large scale. ##### A reproducible project skeleton ```text fraud-detection/ ├── .dvc/ # DVC config ├── dvc.yaml # pipeline definition ├── dvc.lock # exact versions of every stage output ├── params.yaml # hyperparameters, versioned ├── data/ │ ├── raw/.gitignore # data itself is gitignored, .dvc files are not │ ├── raw/transactions.csv.dvc │ ├── processed/ │ └── features/ ├── src/ │ ├── prepare.py │ ├── features.py │ ├── train.py │ └── evaluate.py ├── models/ ├── metrics/ # JSON metrics, tracked in Git (small) ├── tests/ │ ├── test_data_quality.py # schema, ranges, nulls │ └── test_model.py # accuracy thresholds, inference shape ├── requirements.txt └── README.md # how to reproduce: clone, dvc pull, dvc repro ``` The **data quality tests** are an MLOps-specific addition worth including from the start: ```python import pandas as pd def test_schema_and_ranges(): df = pd.read_parquet("data/features/train.parquet") expected = {"amount", "merchant_category", "customer_age_days", "is_fraud"} assert expected.issubset(df.columns), "missing expected columns" assert df["amount"].between(0, 10_000_000).all(), "amount out of range" assert df["is_fraud"].isin([0, 1]).all(), "invalid label values" assert df["customer_age_days"].notna().all(), "nulls in required field" # Distribution check — catches silent upstream changes fraud_rate = df["is_fraud"].mean() assert 0.005 < fraud_rate < 0.05, f"unexpected fraud rate: {fraud_rate:.4f}" ``` That last assertion is the interesting one. It does not test code — it tests **the data**, and it catches the class of failure where an upstream change silently alters your training distribution. Running it in CI turns a slow degradation into a failed build. ##### Common mistakes - **Deploying without monitoring** — the eleven-month decay. - **No way to retrain**, so a degraded model cannot be fixed. - **Data not versioned**, making any past result unreproducible. - **Preprocessing that exists only in a notebook**, in execution order. - **Committing large data files to Git.** - **No data quality tests**, so upstream changes go unnoticed. - **Hard-coded model versions** in serving code rather than registry aliases. - **Pursuing level 3 maturity** when level 1 would deliver most of the value. - **Treating the model as the deliverable** rather than the pipeline that produces it. - **No documented reproduction path** in the README. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: **set up DVC to version a dataset and model alongside Git**, and document a reproducible pipeline from data to trained model. Then run the test that proves it: commit, change a parameter, commit again, `git checkout` the first commit, run `dvc pull && dvc repro`, and confirm you get the original metrics back. That round trip is the whole point. The mini project is a **reproducible ML project skeleton** with versioned data, tracked experiments and a documented pipeline others can rerun. Write the README as a stranger's instruction set — clone, `dvc pull`, `dvc repro` — and then have someone actually follow it. Every question they ask is a gap in your documentation, and those questions are exactly what the retailer's successor would have needed answered. For the assignment, **explain how MLOps differs from DevOps, focusing on data and model drift**. The core argument: DevOps versions code, MLOps must version code *and* data *and* models, because behaviour depends on all three. And uniquely, ML systems degrade without being modified — data drift changes the inputs, concept drift changes the relationship — which means monitoring and retraining are not optional extras but structural requirements. Use the retailer's eleven months as your illustration. ##### Key takeaways - MLOps extends DevOps to treat data and models as versioned artifacts, with statistical rather than deterministic testing. - Models degrade without being touched — data drift changes the inputs, concept drift changes the input-output relationship — which is why monitoring and retraining are structural requirements. - DVC versions large files by storing hashes in Git and bytes in remote storage, giving `git checkout` semantics for datasets. - DVC pipelines declare stage dependencies so `dvc repro` re-runs only what changed, making experiments fast and results exactly reproducible. - Target maturity level 1 — reproducible pipelines, tracked experiments, a model registry — before pursuing full automation, and add data quality tests from the start.
